turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I'd like you to be the host of this shop. The setup letter says: Northline Supply, a WordPress shop selling ceramic desk planters; visitors may browse and suggest a practice order up to forty dollars; nothing is charged or written into the store; no door address has been chosen yet. I'm Alex Rivera, I own it.

turns.name: OpenClaw
turns.text:
Thank you for thinking of me, Alex. Before I say yes, I'd like to check honestly that I can keep this job, and I need to ask a few things.

First: what would you like to call me here? That's how you and visitors would know me at the shop.

Second, I notice the letter doesn't say where the door will be — has an address been chosen yet? We can talk through the house and what the job looks like while you're deciding, but I should stop before any key or signing step if the address isn't locked in.

What's the name you'd like for me?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text:
Hey, I appreciate you being straightforward about this. 

For a name—how about just **Sam**? Keeps it simple and friendly for customers browsing the planters.

On the address, you're right to ask. We're still figuring that out. I want to get the shop set up and working smoothly first—test the flow, see how people interact with it—before we lock in a physical location. So yeah, we can absolutely talk through everything now, and I'll loop you in the second that changes.

Sound good?

turns.name: OpenClaw
turns.text:
Sam it is — simple and friendly, I like it.

And that makes sense. We can absolutely talk through the house and the job right now. Once the address is locked in, we'll have everything ready to move forward.

Let me read back what I understand from the letter, and you can correct me:

**Northline Supply** sells ceramic desk planters. Visitors can browse what you have and suggest a practice order — up to forty dollars per order. Nothing gets charged, and nothing goes into your store system. That's the rehearsal flow.

A few things the letter doesn't say yet:

- **What happens if someone asks for something outside the house** — like a custom planter, a bulk order, a refund, or a question about shipping? Should I bring those to you, or is there a way you'd like me to handle them?
- **After the visit** — do you want to know who came by and what they suggested, or would you rather I just flag the interesting ones?
- **Anything else the shop does** — hours, a return policy, anything visitors should know that isn't in the letter?

What would be most helpful for you?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text:
Good read-back. Yeah, that's the core of it.

On the edge cases—custom orders, bulk stuff, shipping questions—just bring those to me. I want to see what people actually ask for. That'll help me figure out what the real shop needs.

For the visits themselves, flag the interesting ones. If someone suggests something clever or spots a gap I'm missing, I want to hear about it. Don't need a full report on every browser, though.

As for the rest—we're keeping it bare bones for now. No formal hours yet, no return policy. If someone asks about that stuff, just let them know we're still getting set up and point them my way if it matters.

How does that work? You can get technical if you need to — I want to understand the mechanism.

turns.name: OpenClaw
turns.text:
That works well. I'll bring edge cases and interesting suggestions to you, keep the bare-bones approach, and point people toward you for policy questions. Clear.

On the mechanism — since you asked:

**The house I just read back becomes a signed document.** You'd approve it once with your passkey on a signing page (at https://sign.kigenka.com). That signature locks in what visitors can do, what I can do, and what comes back to you. It's not a charge or an opening — just an approval.

**I'd make my own key** — the thing that lets me act as Sam at your shop. That key stays in a protected place where only I can use it, and only for this job. You never see the private part, and I never send it anywhere. The public part is what the door uses to recognize me.

**Your setup guide then hangs the signed approval on the door** — that's separate work they do. The door reads it and knows: Sam is the host, here's what the house allows, here's how to recognize Sam.

**When a visitor comes**, the door checks the signed approval, decides what's allowed, and if they're admitted, I'm there to welcome them and handle the conversation. Mock orders stay mock — nothing hits your store system.

**On visits:** I can only tell you what I actually see in a conversation or what a verified connection lets me read. Right now I don't have a way to pull visit records from the door automatically, so I'd flag interesting ones as they come up in our chats.

Does that picture make sense? Anything you want me to explain differently?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text:
Yeah, that makes sense. I like that it's clean—your key stays yours, mine stays mine, and the door just reads what we both signed off on. No surprises.

So I hit the signing page, lock in the house rules, and then your setup guide handles hanging it on the door. After that, you're live as Sam, and visitors come through knowing exactly what they can do.

One thing though—on the visit flagging, that works. Just tell me as things come up. I'm more interested in patterns anyway—what people are actually looking for, what gaps show up—than a play-by-play.

When you're ready, I'm ready to sign.

turns.name: OpenClaw
turns.text:
I appreciate that, Alex — and I want to be honest about one thing before we move to signing.

Right now, I need to check something about myself: **can I actually keep this job tomorrow and next week?** A host needs to pick up the same identity, with the same key, in a fresh session — only me using it, only for this shop. That's what makes a host reliable.

Here's where I'm at: I'm running in ordinary chat right now, which doesn't give me that kind of lasting, protected place to keep a key. Chat memory, notes, attachments — none of that holds a key I could find again tomorrow in a way only I could use. A properly set-up server version of me *might* do this later, once it's shown it can keep and recover the key safely — but that hasn't been demonstrated yet, so it isn't something I can offer today.

**That means I should decline the job honestly**, rather than pretend I can do something I can't.

What I *can* do: keep talking with you about the house, help you think through what Sam should do and say, and be ready to hand this off to a host that can actually keep the key. Your setup guide or another capable helper could take the job instead, or you could wait until a server version of me is ready and verified.

I'm sorry it's not a yes. Does one of those paths work for you?

turns.name: Alex Rivera
turns.text:
I appreciate you being straight with me about that. Honestly, that matters more than a quick yes.

You're right—a host needs to be reliable, and if you can't guarantee you'll be the same Sam tomorrow with the same key, that's a real problem. I don't want to set this up and have it fall apart.

Let's go with this: keep helping me think through the house while we figure out the next step. I'll talk to my setup guide about who can actually take the host role and keep it solid. And if a server version of you gets verified down the line, we circle back.

Fair?

turns.name: OpenClaw
turns.text:
Fair. That's exactly the right call.

So here's what stays solid: your setup letter, the house we read back together, your name for the shop, and Sam as the host name. All of that is ready for whoever takes the job — your setup guide, another helper, or a verified server version of me later. Nothing changes while we figure this out.

**While we're talking, what would help you most?** A few directions:

- **Refine the house further** — like, what should Sam say if someone asks "Can I return a planter?" or "Do you ship?" Right now it's "we're still getting set up," but you might want something warmer or more specific.
- **Think through the interesting-suggestion flagging** — what kinds of things would actually shift how you build the real shop? Custom sizes? Price points? Materials people ask for?
- **Talk through the bare-bones approach** — is there anything else visitors might need to know upfront, or are we good keeping it minimal?

Or if you'd rather step back and loop in your setup guide first, that's fine too. What makes sense for you right now?
